# `node/no-unpublished-require`

**Published files require only what is published**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pack** | `@codelaw/rules-node` (npm) |
| **Languages** | JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX |
| **Turned on by** | `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error` |
| **Severity when named without one** | `error` |
| **Options** | none — severity only |
| **Fix** | `manual` — no automatic fix; the steps are under *How to fix* (whether to publish the file, move the dependency or move the code is the package owner's choice) |
| **Stability** | `preview` — runs only with `preview = true` |
| **Since** | 0.1.0 |
| **Scope** | project — reads the whole repository through the project graph, not one file at a time |
| **Ported from** | `eslint-plugin-n/no-unpublished-require` |

## What it checks

In a package that is not `private` and lists `files`, a file `npm publish` packs requires neither a project file it doesn't pack nor a package that is only a `devDependency`.

**Why:** the published package then fails to load for its users: the file isn't in the tarball, or the devDependency isn't installed.

## Configuration

Everything below goes in `codelaw.toml` at the repo root. The same keys work as `[tool.codelaw]` in `pyproject.toml` or `"codelaw"` in `package.json` ([SR-CONFIG](../../../records/0110_config.md)).

### Turn it on

**Install the pack** (`codelaw init` does it for the languages it finds):

```bash
npm install --save-dev @codelaw/rules-node
```

**Then extend a preset that turns it on** — `codelaw:node/recommended` sets it to `error`:

```toml
preview = true                        # pack rules are preview today
extends = ["codelaw:node/recommended"]
```

- **A rule exists only once its pack is loaded** through `extends`; naming it in `[rules]` without that is an unknown rule id (exit 2).
- **Without `preview = true`** the rule is skipped and codelaw warns that it is preview.

### Severity

```toml
[rules]
"node/no-unpublished-require" = "warn"    # error | warn | info | off
```

- **`error`** fails the run (exit 1) · **`warn`** fails only with `--max-warnings N` · **`info`** never fails · **`off`** turns it off.
- **Naming it with a severity turns it on** even when no preset does.

### For a group of files

A `[scope.<name>]` gives some files their own setting, applied after `[rules]` — the `tests` scope `codelaw:js/recommended` ships (`**/*.test.*`, `**/*.spec.*`); naming it extends it, so its files stay:

```toml
[scope.tests]
rules = { "node/no-unpublished-require" = "off" }
```

A scope's `remap` changes whole severities in its files, after everything else: `remap = { error = "warn" }` never fails the run there.

### Warn locally, fail in CI

The `ci` profile runs when `CI` is set; `local` otherwise; `--profile <name>` or `CODELAW_PROFILE` picks one.

```toml
[profile.local.rules]
"node/no-unpublished-require" = "warn"

[profile.ci.rules]
"node/no-unpublished-require" = "error"
```

### In `pyproject.toml` or `package.json`

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[tool.codelaw.rules]
"node/no-unpublished-require" = { severity = "warn" }
```

```json
{
  "codelaw": {
    "rules": {
      "node/no-unpublished-require": {"severity": "warn"}
    }
  }
}
```

### Silence one finding

An inline `codelaw-ignore` always needs a reason; `expires=`, `warn_days=` and `by=` date it ([SR-LINTER](../../../records/0106_linter.md) decision 6).

- **JavaScript:** `// codelaw-ignore node/no-unpublished-require: <reason>`
- **Dated:** `// codelaw-ignore node/no-unpublished-require expires=2026-12-31 by=you@example.com: <reason>`

### Keep today's findings, fail on new ones

```bash
codelaw baseline add --rule node/no-unpublished-require --expires 2026-12-31 --reason "<why>"
```

See [SR-BASELINE](../../../records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md).

### See what applies

```bash
codelaw explain node/no-unpublished-require       # what it wants, why, how to fix
codelaw check --rule node/no-unpublished-require  # only this rule
codelaw config --print --for <file>               # the resolved setting, and where it came from
```

## How to fix

1. Add the required file to `files` in the nearest `package.json`, move the package from `devDependencies` to `dependencies`, or move the `require()` out of the published code.

## Examples

### JavaScript

#### Don't

```js files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.js", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.js
const { fixtures } = require("../test/fixtures");
console.log(fixtures);
// test/fixtures.js
export const fixtures = [];
```

#### Do

```js files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.js", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.js
const { fixtures } = require("./fixtures");
console.log(fixtures);
// lib/fixtures.js
export const fixtures = [];
```

### JSX

#### Don't

```jsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.jsx", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.jsx
const { fixtures } = require("../test/fixtures");
export const App = () => <p>{String(fixtures)}</p>;
// test/fixtures.jsx
export const fixtures = [];
```

#### Do

```jsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.jsx", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.jsx
const { fixtures } = require("./fixtures");
export const App = () => <p>{String(fixtures)}</p>;
// lib/fixtures.jsx
export const fixtures = [];
```
